title: How authoritarian states are building an international market for digital surveillance
sourceTitle: How authoritarian states are building an international market for digital surveillance
attribution: Global Voices — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Authoritarian countries are using new technology to control their people. This includes cameras that recognize faces, systems that watch social media, and digital IDs. These tools are all coming together into one big system of control. This system helps governments watch people in real time and also find out what they did in the past. One example is Russia.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: CCTV Cameras

pages.text: A 15-year-old girl named Sonya was punished for writing “Navalny” on a bus stop. A man named Yuri was also punished for writing “No to War” on buildings. Both were found using surveillance cameras. Moscow has many cameras, and it is one of the cities outside China with the most cameras per person.

China also has many cameras, with almost one camera for every two people. These countries are sharing and selling these technologies. China, Russia, Iran, and others are involved. Russia is trying to sell its AI models to countries in the Global South. However, Russian AI models are not as good as American or Chinese ones.

China, on the other hand, makes its language models open, which means others can use and change them. China also sells “smart city” systems that watch citizens closely. These systems are used in places like Western Asia, where many countries are authoritarian. Iran uses both Chinese and Russian surveillance technology.

For example, Iran bought a Russian facial recognition system called FindFace. People in Iran have been fined for not wearing a hijab, and their social media posts have been used against them. This shows how these technologies help governments stop protests before they even start.
Russia and China are also working together on AI research and development, especially for drones and surveillance.

According to estimates by Comparitech , two of the ten cities outside China with the highest number of cameras per person are Russian: Moscow and St. Petersburg.

At the same time, an investigation by Le Monde and Forbidden Stories showed that Iran acquired the Russian facial recognition system FindFace , developed by NtechLab, through Iranian intermediary companies.

pages.text: Authoritarian governments are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) and related digital technologies to maintain political control. This involves integrating various tools such as facial recognition cameras, video analytics, biometric databases, digital IDs, social media monitoring, and Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) systems into a unified infrastructure.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: CCTV Cameras

pages.text: This comprehensive system allows states to not only monitor citizens in real time but also to reconstruct their past activities, connections, habits, and political engagements. The primary concern is that AI makes repression faster and less visible, as citizens become aware that their actions can be retroactively identified, reducing the need for overt displays of force.

Examples from Russia illustrate this trend. Sonya, a 15-year-old from Stavropol Krai, was sentenced to 70 hours of compulsory labor in June 2026 for writing “Navalny” on a bus stop in a district monitored by the Center for Combating Extremism.

Similarly, Yuri, a pensioner from Astrakhan, received three years of restricted freedom for writing “No to War” on buildings, identified through surveillance footage. Moscow, along with St. Petersburg, ranks among the top ten cities outside China with the highest number of cameras per person, part of a complex digital urban ecosystem that includes video surveillance, AI, big data, and the “internet of things.” This digital authoritarianism is not developing in isolation but through an international market for surveillance technologies.

Countries like China, Russia, Iran, and Belarus, along with associated companies, are actively selling and exchanging AI infrastructure tools used for repression. Western technologies are also acquired and utilized by these regimes. China has become a leading exporter of “smart city” systems, which involve extensive surveillance capabilities like video monitoring, wiretapping, and facial recognition.

These systems are supplied to countries in the Global South, particularly in Western Asia, where many territories are classified as authoritarian. Russia has also sought to export its AI models, with Sberbank Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin stating in June 2026 that the company was offering countries in the Global South access to Russian AI models designed to incorporate “local values.” However, Russian generative AI models, such as GigaChat and YandexGPT, are reportedly less advanced than their American and Chinese counterparts and struggle with generating Cyrillic text.

Despite this, Russia continues to cooperate with China on AI research and development, particularly in areas like drone technology and mass surveillance, and shares technologies with North Korea, which has tested AI-guided cruise missiles. Iran provides a case study of this international exchange, relying heavily on Chinese technologies for internet control, including facial recognition and filtering equipment from companies like Huawei and Hikvision.

Iran also acquired the Russian facial recognition system FindFace through intermediaries, reselling it to state-linked entities. Citizens have faced consequences for online activities and non-compliance with regulations, with investigators using extensive dossiers of social media posts.

This demonstrates how AI systems aid authorities in detecting early signals of protest, such as unusual online activity or activist connections, effectively suppressing dissent before it fully materializes.

pages.text: Authoritarian regimes are increasingly leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) as a critical technology for political survival, integrating facial recognition cameras, video analytics, biometric databases, digital IDs, social media monitoring, Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) systems, and public service platforms into a cohesive infrastructure of control.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: CCTV Cameras

pages.text: This sophisticated system enables real-time citizen observation and the retroactive reconstruction of past movements, connections, habits, communications, and political activities. The inherent risk lies in AI and related technologies accelerating and obscuring repression, as the state's need to overtly demonstrate force diminishes when citizens are aware of their potential for retroactive identification. Russia exemplifies this digital authoritarianism.

Sonya, a 15-year-old from Stavropol Krai, received a sentence of 70 hours of compulsory labor in June 2026 for writing “Navalny” on a bus stop in a district under surveillance by the Center for Combating Extremism. Similarly, Yuri, an Astrakhan pensioner, was given three years of restricted freedom for anti-war graffiti, identified via surveillance footage.

Moscow has transcended the conventional “smart city” concept, evolving into a complex digital urban ecosystem encompassing video surveillance, AI, big data, and the “internet of things.” Comparitech estimates place Moscow and St. Petersburg among the top ten non-Chinese cities globally for camera density per person, while China itself approaches a ratio of one camera for every two individuals, representing the world’s largest mass-surveillance system.

The development of modern digital authoritarianism is not insular but driven by an international exchange of technologies, standards, and practices. China, Russia, Iran, Belarus, Venezuela, and various countries in Africa, Western and Central Asia, along with their associated companies, actively trade and sell AI infrastructure tools for repressive purposes. Western technologies are also procured and integrated by these regimes.

China, through its Digital Silk Road initiative launched in 2017, has made the export of digital infrastructure a cornerstone of its foreign policy, promoting “smart city” systems that facilitate comprehensive citizen surveillance, including video monitoring, wiretapping, internet censorship, and ethnic profiling, particularly in the Global South. Russia, despite its technological dependence on China, also seeks to export its AI capabilities.

Sberbank Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin indicated in June 2026 that the company was offering countries in the Global South access to Russian AI models, such as GigaChat and YandexGPT, designed to incorporate “local values.” However, IT expert Alexander Isavnin notes that Russian generative AI models lag behind American and Chinese counterparts and struggle with Cyrillic text generation.

Nevertheless, Russia and China are deepening cooperation in AI technological research and development, particularly for drone training and mass surveillance, with joint laboratories established in November 2025. Russia also collaborates with North Korea, testing AI in military operations, where North Korean weapons are evaluated in Ukraine, and operational data is reciprocated to enhance North Korean AI-guided systems.

Iran's internet control architecture heavily relies on Chinese technologies, as revealed by an Article 19 report in February 2026, which identified suppliers like Huawei, ZTE, Hikvision, and Tiandy for facial recognition and internet filtering equipment. Concurrently, Iran acquired the Russian facial recognition system FindFace, developed by NtechLab, through intermediary companies, subsequently reselling it to state-linked entities including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Ministry of Intelligence.

Instances such as fines for women not wearing hijabs in cars since 2019, and the detention of artist Taraneh M. during the “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests, where investigators presented extensive dossiers of her social media posts dating back five years, underscore how these integrated AI systems enable authorities to detect and suppress dissent at its nascent stages, often before it fully materializes.

title: Norway’s Telenor telecom faces lawsuit for giving user data to Myanmar junta
sourceTitle: Norway’s Telenor telecom faces lawsuit for giving user data to Myanmar junta
attribution: Global Voices — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Telenor, a telecom company from Norway, is being sued for giving customer information to Myanmar's military government. This is the first time a telecom company might be held responsible for not keeping user data safe from a strict government. Telenor worked in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022 and had 18 million customers.
pages.caption: Myanmar Telenor

imageProvenance.credit: Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022. Photo by Bjoertvedt. Source: Wikipedia.

pages.text: After the military took over in February 2021, Telenor was asked to share customer data. Telenor decided to leave Myanmar, but some groups worried that its business would be sold to a company connected to the military. In April 2026, people from Myanmar sued Telenor in Norway.

They said Telenor shared their private information, like 1,253 phone numbers, call records, and locations, with the military. One person suing is Tha Zin, whose husband, Phyo Zeya Thaw, was arrested and killed after his account information was accessed. Tha Zin said, "I lost my husband. It is not just a wife losing her husband.

It is also a loss to the movement." Telenor said it had to give the data to protect its employees in Myanmar. They said their workers could have been jailed, hurt, or even killed if they didn't follow orders. However, groups like Civicus believe companies should not help with human rights abuses.
This case could make other companies think about their responsibilities when working in dangerous places.

If successful, the case would be the first ever to hold a telecom company accountable for failing to protect user data from being misused by an authoritarian regime.
The complaint alleged that Telenor shared at least 1,253 phone numbers with the regime.

pages.text: Norway-based multinational telecom company Telenor is currently facing legal action for its alleged role in providing sensitive customer data to Myanmar's military government. This landmark case, if successful, would mark the first instance of a telecom company being held accountable for failing to safeguard user data from potential misuse by an authoritarian regime.
pages.caption: Myanmar Telenor

imageProvenance.credit: Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022. Photo by Bjoertvedt. Source: Wikipedia.

pages.text: Telenor operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022, serving 18 million subscribers. Following the February 2021 coup, Telenor faced significant pressure as the junta demanded compliance with its surveillance and content blocking directives. While Telenor ultimately decided to exit Myanmar, civil society groups voiced strong objections regarding the proposed sale of its local operations to a company with known links to the military regime.

In December 2024, activist group Justice For Myanmar initially filed a complaint against Telenor in Norway for breaching the Sanctions Act. Although this was rejected, the complaint was refiled in October 2025, adding a charge of aiding and abetting crimes against humanity.

Given that the Norwegian state holds a 54-percent stake in Telenor, the Norwegian Parliament initiated an investigation into Telenor's Myanmar operations in December 2025. A parliamentary leader questioned, "We must uncover how a state-owned company could cooperate with a brutal military regime (by handing over) customer information about the opposition [in Myanmar]." In April 2026, a civil class action lawsuit was filed against Telenor in Norway by Myanmar citizens.

The lawsuit claims Telenor shared sensitive personal data, including at least 1,253 phone numbers, call logs, location data, names, addresses, ID numbers, Facebook, and bank accounts linked to mobile numbers, with the junta. Among the complainants is Tha Zin, the widow of rapper and lawmaker Phyo Zeya Thaw, who was arrested, convicted on a trumped-up charge, and executed by the junta.

Tha Zin stated her husband's arrest occurred immediately after his account information was accessed by the regime, emphasizing, "I lost my husband. It is not just a wife losing her husband. It is also a loss to the movement. It is also a loss to democracy because my husband was committed to democracy and a youth leader.

Losing him means a loss to the country." Telenor has stated it is cooperating with authorities, asserting that it needed to defend its employees in Myanmar, who faced risks of imprisonment, torture, or the death penalty if military orders were not followed. However, civil society organizations, including Civicus, argue that companies should not facilitate human rights abuses.
This case is seen as a crucial step towards challenging impunity and reminding companies of their ongoing human rights responsibilities, even when exiting high-risk markets.

pages.text: Telenor, the Norway-based multinational telecom company, is currently embroiled in legal proceedings concerning its alleged complicity in the transfer of sensitive customer data to Myanmar's military government. This case represents a potentially groundbreaking precedent, as it seeks to establish accountability for a telecom company's failure to protect user data from exploitation by an authoritarian regime.
pages.caption: Myanmar Telenor

imageProvenance.credit: Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022. Photo by Bjoertvedt. Source: Wikipedia.

pages.text: Telenor maintained operations in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022, accumulating 18 million subscribers. Following the February 2021 coup, the company faced intense pressure from the junta, which issued directives demanding compliance with its surveillance and content blocking mandates.

While Telenor ultimately opted to divest from Myanmar, its decision was met with significant opposition from civil society groups, who expressed grave concerns that the sale of its local operations would benefit a company with demonstrable ties to the military regime.

In December 2024, the activist organization Justice For Myanmar lodged a complaint against Telenor in Norway, citing a breach of the Sanctions Act. Although initially rejected, the complaint was refiled in October 2025, augmented with an additional charge of aiding and abetting crimes against humanity.

Given the Norwegian state's 54-percent ownership stake in Telenor, the Norwegian Parliament initiated an investigation into the company's Myanmar operations in December 2025. The leader of the parliamentary disciplinary committee articulated the imperative to "uncover how a state-owned company could cooperate with a brutal military regime (by handing over) customer information about the opposition [in Myanmar]." April 2026 saw the filing of a civil class action lawsuit against Telenor in Norway by Myanmar citizens.

The complaint meticulously detailed allegations that Telenor shared a minimum of 1,253 phone numbers with the regime, alongside call logs, location data, names, addresses, ID numbers, and associated Facebook and bank accounts. Among the plaintiffs is Tha Zin, the widow of the prominent rapper and lawmaker Phyo Zeya Thaw, who was arrested on a fabricated charge, convicted, and subsequently executed by the junta.

Tha Zin recounted her husband's arrest immediately following the regime's access to his account information, lamenting, "I lost my husband. It is not just a wife losing her husband. It is also a loss to the movement. It is also a loss to democracy because my husband was committed to democracy and a youth leader.

Losing him means a loss to the country." Lawyer Jan Magne Langseth summarized the core of the complaint, asserting that "Telenor ASA in Norway clearly contributed to the practice of handing over user data, despite the inherent risks for its customers in Myanmar.

We have evidence of cases where the team at HQ expressly recommended the data to be handed over." In September 2026, Norway’s National Criminal Investigation Service and interior security service conducted a search of Telenor’s offices in connection with these charges.

Justice for Myanmar spokesperson Yadanar Maung welcomed the investigation, highlighting that "Telenor’s transfer of spyware to a military-linked company and sharing of sensitive data with the military junta was extensively documented." Telenor, in statements to the media, affirmed its cooperation with the ongoing investigation, while simultaneously emphasizing the critical need to protect its employees in Myanmar.

The company contended that refusing demands from military authorities could have resulted in severe repercussions, including "imprisonment, torture or the death penalty." Telenor's media relations director, David Fidjeland, reiterated this stance, stating, "Our employees risked imprisonment, torture or the death penalty if the military authorities’ orders were not complied with.

We found that we had no real choice and that we could not put our employees’ lives at risk." While acknowledging the junta's brutality, Telenor maintained that an employer cannot issue instructions that directly imperil employees' lives. Civil society groups view this investigation as a significant stride in combating impunity.

Civicus underscored that companies bear a responsibility not to enable human rights abuses. Faiz Naeem, Asia Pacific policy analyst at Access Now, characterized the Telenor case as a stark reminder for technology and telecom companies operating in high-risk environments: "leaving a market does not mean leaving your human rights responsibilities behind." The civil class action lawsuit is seeking damages of EUR 9,000 (roughly USD 10,500) per affected customer.

title: After flood disasters, Nepal needs clear numbers on aid and a reconstruction plan
sourceTitle: After flood disasters, Nepal needs clear numbers on aid and a reconstruction plan
attribution: Global Voices — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Nepal has faced many floods and landslides recently. On October 11, 2026, a new flood hit Chumnubri, Gorkha. This happened after a big flood in Bhotekoshi, which affected Rasuwa and Nuwakot. These disasters make life hard for people who live near natural dangers. The floods in Nuwakot have ruined beautiful places that tourists liked.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Nepal glacier collapse and flood  after   55504451912

pages.text: Roads, bridges, and power stations are gone. Many homes are destroyed or damaged. Kyodo News says 7,500 homes were affected, and fixing everything will cost USD 4.77 billion. The government is now trying to rebuild and help people recover. Nepal has received some money for help, USD 24.89 million, but more has been promised, USD 50.47 million.

It is important to know where all the money goes. Countries like India, China, the United States, and the UAE are helping. But many people still need homes and jobs. They need help to rebuild their lives and feel safe again from future floods. Bhotekoshi (बोतेकोशी): A river in Nepal known for flash floods.
Chumnubri (चुम्नुब्री): A rural municipality in Gorkha District, Nepal. Nuwakot (नुवाकोट): A district in Nepal, heavily affected by recent disasters.

keyVocabulary.meaningVi: Một con sông ở Nepal nổi tiếng với lũ quét.
Một đô thị nông thôn ở huyện Gorkha, Nepal.
Một huyện ở Nepal, bị ảnh hưởng nặng nề bởi các thảm họa gần đây.

evidence: Forty-six days later, just when Nepal was trying to recover from the Bhotekoshi flash flood , which struck the Nepal–Tibet border regions, affecting Rasuwa and Nuwakot, another landslide-induced flood hit Chumnubri, Gorkha, on October 11, 2026.
Kyodo News reports via AP that 7,500 homes were damaged or completely destroyed, with costs of recovery hitting USD 4.77 billion.

Nepal’s Ministry of Finance’s foreign assistance tracker shows that Nepal has received USD 24.89 million in disaster relief funds. Such tracking can help bring transparency to the collection and distribution of aid. The Prime Minister's Office separately reported that USD 50.47 million of assistance (cash, materials, and teams) had been pledged.

pages.text: Nepal is facing ongoing challenges from a series of natural disasters. On October 11, 2026, a landslide-induced flood struck Chumnubri, Gorkha, just weeks after the Bhotekoshi flash flood impacted the Nepal–Tibet border regions, including Rasuwa and Nuwakot.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Nepal glacier collapse and flood  after   55504451912

pages.text: These events have intensified the struggles of communities already living with the constant threat of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities. The recent climate-related disaster in Nuwakot has severely damaged a once-thriving tourist area.

Its natural beauty and economic opportunities have been lost, with settlements reduced to rubble and critical infrastructure, such as roads, bridges, and hydropower facilities, washed away. The official death toll remains unconfirmed. Beyond the physical destruction, there is a significant human cost, with countless stories of broken dreams, lost livelihoods, and buried memories.

Families are struggling to survive without loved ones, and communities face an uncertain future as they try to rebuild from what little remains. The scale of reconstruction is immense. Damage extends beyond homes to farms and local businesses. According to Kyodo News, 7,500 homes were either damaged or completely destroyed, with recovery costs estimated at USD 4.77 billion.

The government has shifted its focus from emergency relief to long-term rehabilitation and reconstruction, acknowledging the risks of potential glacial outburst floods (GLOFs) and other hazards. The destruction of transport links has isolated surviving communities, hindering reconstruction efforts and increasing their vulnerability. Joint efforts are underway to restore damaged infrastructure and vital services.

However, there is a notable difference between pledged assistance and funds actually received. Nepal’s Ministry of Finance reports USD 24.89 million in disaster relief funds received, while the Prime Minister's Office indicates USD 50.47 million in pledged assistance. This discrepancy highlights the need for transparency in aid distribution.

While India, China, the United States, the UAE, and international financial institutions like the Asian Development Bank have committed funds, a formal update on longer-term reconstruction plans is still pending. Most aid currently addresses immediate needs like medical assistance, food, and temporary shelters.

The challenge for affected communities is not only to rebuild physical structures but also to restore livelihoods, public services, and a sense of security against recurring environmental threats. Nuwakot (नुवाकोट): Một huyện ở Nepal, bị ảnh hưởng nặng nề bởi các thảm họa gần đây.

Herrera said the book shows that Chabacano is still alive and that people are working to keep it going through writing. The book's title talks about changes in Zamboanga City. It calls Zamboanga the “City of Flowers.” Herrera noted that many poems use a lot of Spanish words. He hopes the book will help people accept different ways of writing in Chabacano. He also hopes this book will lead to more books in the future, even though it is hard to find Chabacano poets.

pages.text: A new poetry anthology, “Sombra y Luz,” is promoting Chabacano, a unique language in the Philippines. Chabacano is one of the Philippines’ one hundred seventy languages and is widely spoken in Zamboanga, standing out as Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language. The Philippines was under Spanish colonial rule for over three centuries.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Zamboanga City's Sunset

pages.text: However, the Spanish language was primarily used by the elite, friars, and colonial rulers. It was only in Zamboanga that a Spanish-based creole language, Chabacano, developed. In 2018, Jerome Herrera, creator of the blog Bien Chabacano, which is dedicated to promoting and documenting Chavacano de Zamboanga, initiated a book project.

He invited writers to submit poems for an anthology, leading to the launch of “Sombra y Luz” in July. This collection features twenty-three poems by ten authors, primarily exploring themes of love, family, and Zamboangueño identity.

Herrera stated that “The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a literary language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.” He also explained that the book's title, “Sombra y Luz” (Shadow and Light), aims to convey the contrasts and changes occurring in Zamboanga City.

The cover art, featuring an American-era style lamppost and bougainvilleas, offers a nostalgic reference to the city's past, when it was known as the Ciudad de Flores, or “City of Flowers.” One poem by Jayline Gonzales-Barredo, included in the anthology, vividly describes the city's natural beauty, mentioning “Maga pajaro que ta vola-vola, Na maga rama de pono ta queda, Alegre con uno y otro ta grita-grita, Twit!

Twit! Twit! Entero el dia.” This translates to birds flying and singing joyfully throughout the day, enriching life in the city. Herrera noted the significant presence of Spanish words in the submitted poems. He acknowledged the ongoing debate about the ideal form of Chabacano poetry, with some preferring a strong Spanish influence and others favoring everyday conversational Chabacano.

He believes that for poetry, an “idealistic manner” with more Spanish words is acceptable, as writers often use them for formality and poetic effect. He hopes the anthology will encourage greater acceptance of the diverse ways Chabacano is used, stating, “For a very long time, people have been putting Chabacano inside a box.

I hope that these books open up conversations regarding Chabacano literature and make people receptive to different kinds of writing styles in Chabacano.” The poem “Escribi Chavacano, Conversa Chabacano” exemplifies this approach, celebrating Chabacano as a living language and highlighting the coexistence of its two accepted spellings, Chavacano and Chabacano, thus showcasing the richness of its written tradition.
Despite the challenge of finding Chabacano contributors, Herrera hopes this anthology is just the beginning, aiming for future literary initiatives and a second volume.

pages.text: A recently published poetry anthology, “Sombra y Luz,” is playing a pivotal role in the promotion and preservation of Chabacano, a distinctive language indigenous to the Philippines. As one of the Philippines’ one hundred seventy languages, Chabacano is predominantly spoken in the southern city of Zamboanga and holds the unique distinction of being Asia’s sole Spanish-based creole language.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Zamboanga City's Sunset

pages.text: Historically, the Philippines endured over three centuries of Spanish colonial rule. However, the Spanish language itself remained largely confined to the societal elite, religious friars, and the colonial administration. It was exclusively within Zamboanga that a Spanish-based creole language, Chabacano, managed to flourish and develop.

The impetus for this anthology originated in 2018 with Jerome Herrera, the founder of Bien Chabacano, a dedicated blog focused on documenting and advocating for Chavacano de Zamboanga. Herrera initiated a collaborative book project, inviting writers to contribute poems for compilation.

This endeavor culminated in the July launch of “Sombra y Luz,” a collection featuring twenty-three poems penned by ten authors. The thematic core of these works largely revolves around love, familial bonds, and the intricate facets of Zamboangueño identity.

Herrera articulated that “The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a literary language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.” He further elaborated that the anthology’s title, “Sombra y Luz” (Shadow and Light), is intended to metaphorically represent the dynamic contrasts and transformations evident within Zamboanga City.

The book’s cover art, which depicts an American-era style lamppost and bougainvilleas, serves as a poignant, nostalgic homage to the city’s historical appellation as the Ciudad de Flores, or “City of Flowers.” The anthology includes a poem by Jayline Gonzales-Barredo that vividly captures the city’s natural vibrancy.

The lines “Maga pajaro que ta vola-vola, Na maga rama de pono ta queda, Alegre con uno y otro ta grita-grita, Twit! Twit! Twit! Entero el dia” translate to a joyful depiction of birds in flight and song, enriching the urban soundscape. In an interview, Herrera observed a pronounced prevalence of Spanish vocabulary within the submitted poems.

He acknowledged the ongoing scholarly and communal discourse regarding the quintessential form of Chabacano poetry, noting a divergence between those who favor a strong Spanish lexical presence and those who advocate for a style more reflective of everyday Chabacano conversation.

Herrera posited that for poetic expression, an “idealistic manner” incorporating more Spanish words is justifiable, as Chabacano writers frequently employ them to imbue their works with a sense of formality and heightened poeticism. He expressed a profound hope that the anthology will foster greater inclusivity and acceptance of the diverse stylistic manifestations of Chabacano.

Herrera stated, “For a very long time, people have been putting Chabacano inside a box. I hope that these books open up conversations regarding Chabacano literature and make people receptive to different kinds of writing styles in Chabacano.” This inclusive philosophy is notably embodied in the poem “Escribi Chavacano, Conversa Chabacano,” which not only celebrates Chabacano as a vibrant, living language but also underscores the harmonious coexistence of its two accepted orthographic forms, Chavacano and Chabacano, thereby illustrating the richness and adaptability of its written tradition.

Despite the inherent challenges in identifying and engaging Chabacano literary contributors, Herrera remains optimistic that this anthology represents merely the genesis of broader literary initiatives, with aspirations for a subsequent volume in the future.
